newsitem.title: UK: IGC notes careful balance on grain export subsidy.
newsitem.headline: IGC notes careful balance on grain export subsidy.

text.p: Grain subsidy levels seem unlikely for now to cause a rift between the big exporters, Germain Denis, executive director of the International Grains Council (IGC), said on Wednesday. "I believe the situation will remain as it is for the time being," he told Reuters, adding that the direction of prices would be clearer when indications on the size of the 1997 harvest emerge in coming months.
European Union (EU) efforts to avoid a spat with the United States on subsidies were noted by grain nations meeting under the IGC umbrella this week.
The London-based IGC grouping importers and exporters said developing countries that rely on food imports also expressed concern about recent price fluctuations in wheat.
Prices have tumbled from historic highs earlier this year in as an ample 1996 harvest shifted the supply scenario from shortage to surpluses in a matter of just months.
The EU, after a bumper harvest, has fine-tuned export subsidies to try to avoid vexing the United States while allowing exports to flow at a reasonable speed.

But grain exporters who point to aggressive sales by Argentina to traditional EU outlets are pressing the European Commission to abandon using U.S. wheat as a benchmark and compete instead with cheaper alternatives.

The IGC said in a statement: "The apparent determination of governments of major exporting countries to refrain from market intervention that could exacerbate recent downward price movements was noted." Last week, the EU granted the export of 198,000 tonnes of wheat at a refund of 18 Ecus per tonne, valuing its wheat at $154 per tonne fob for December or January shipment.
But Argentine wheat is worth around $130-133 fob.
